 "id":"Q94",
 "sourceFile":"The Impact of Weekly Acceleration and Deceleration Loads on Neuromuscular Performance in Soccer - A Session-to-Session Analysis.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title 'The Impact of Weekly Acceleration and Deceleration Loads on Neuromuscular Performance in Soccer: A Session-to-Session Analysis' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Training & Performance",
 "domains":["Training & Performance","Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Athletic Training","Coaching","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Soccer"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Healthy Athletes","Youth / Adolescent"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Descriptive repeated-measures observational study of 39 male under-19 outfield soccer players from two teams, followed over two consecutive microcycles. GNSS acceleration and deceleration counts were recorded for each session, with countermovement jump (CMJ), isometric hamstring strength and DOMS measured before and after training. Post-training CMJ and hamstring strength were lower than pre-training on every day, with the largest drops on MD-4 and MD-5 (about 8% each), and DOMS peaked on MD-3. No daily acceleration or deceleration count correlated significantly with the pre-post change in CMJ or hamstring strength.",
 "screeningLimitations":"A single pair of under-19 teams, convenience sampling, two weeks of data, and two trials per test limit generalisability and precision. Only acceleration and deceleration counts were analysed, and the correlations are cross-sectional, so they cannot detect lagged effects the authors themselves suggest.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Reading the absence of same-session correlations as proof that acceleration and deceleration load does not drive fatigue, or as a reason to ignore session loads.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"Tan B, Hu A, Zheng Y. The Impact of Weekly Acceleration and Deceleration Loads on Neuromuscular Performance in Soccer: A Session-to-Session Analysis. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2025;24:851-860.",
   "doi":"10.52082/jssm.2025.851",
   "abstract":"This study examined weekly variations in accelerations, decelerations and neuromuscular performance in male under-19 soccer players, and whether accumulated acceleration and deceleration loads relate to neuromuscular changes across a weekly microcycle. Thirty-nine outfield players were monitored by GNSS over two consecutive weeks, with countermovement jump (CMJ), hamstring strength (HS) and delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) measured before and after training. CMJ and HS fell significantly after training on all five days, most on MD-4 and MD-5, and DOMS peaked on MD-3. No significant correlations were found between daily acceleration or deceleration counts and changes in CMJ or HS.",
   "tldr":"In 39 under-19 players, CMJ and hamstring strength fell after training on every day and were lowest on MD-4 and MD-5, but single-day acceleration and deceleration counts did not predict those drops. Plan late-week loads using the cumulative pattern rather than one session's counts.",
   "methods":"Descriptive, repeated-measures observational study over two consecutive weeks with two under-19 teams in provincial competition. Accelerations and decelerations were counted by a 10 Hz GNSS vest for each training session. CMJ height and isometric hamstring strength were measured 30 minutes before and 15 minutes after each session, and a 0 to 6 DOMS scale was completed each morning before training. Values were averaged by day relative to match day, then analysed with repeated-measures ANOVA, Bonferroni post hoc tests and Pearson correlations.",
   "findings":"Post-training CMJ and hamstring strength were significantly below pre-training on every day (p < 0.001). The largest drops were on MD-4 (CMJ -7.9%, hamstring -7.9%) and MD-5 (CMJ -7.8%, hamstring -7.9%). Pre-training CMJ and hamstring strength declined from MD-1 to MD-4. DOMS peaked on MD-3 (mean 1.04). Acceleration and deceleration counts were highest on MD-4 (means 44.00 and 43.65). No daily count was significantly correlated with the post-pre change in CMJ or HS; MD-5 showed non-significant trends of r = -0.27 to -0.32 (p = 0.050 to 0.092).",
   "limitations":"Observational design with no control group, so the findings describe association only. The sample is modest, restricted to two youth male teams, and chosen by convenience. Daily values were averaged across the two weeks before analysis, and the unit of analysis for the correlations is not clearly stated. Only two trials per test were used, and only acceleration and deceleration counts were analysed. The MD-5 correlation trends did not reach significance, and the authors note that a same-day design cannot capture lagged effects.",
   "practicalImplications":"Track CMJ and hamstring strength before and after sessions across the week, and plan MD-4 and MD-5 loads with recovery in mind, since those were the lowest-performing days in this group. Do not use a single session's acceleration or deceleration count to predict same-day decline, because this study found no link. Combine GNSS counts with other load and wellness measures.",
   "athleteDev":"Use pre- and post-session CMJ and hamstring tests as a weekly fatigue check, and watch midweek soreness, which peaked on MD-3 here. Do not use session acceleration or deceleration counts alone to judge an individual player's same-day readiness, since the study found no relationship.",
   "rtp":"Not applicable to return to sport. Players recovering from injury were excluded, so the results cannot set return-to-play criteria or load limits for injured players."
 }
}

 The Inﬂuence of Exercise Modality on Training Load Management
 Øyvind Sandbakk, Thomas Haugen, and Gertjan Ettema
 Purpose: To provide novel insight regarding the inﬂuence of exercise modality on training load management by (1) providing a
 theoretical framework for the impact of physiological and biomechanical mechanisms associated with different exercise
 modalities on training load management in endurance exercise and (2) comparing effort-matched low-intensity training sessions
 performed by top-level athletes in endurance sports with similar energy demands. Practical Applications and Conclusions: The
 ability to perform endurance training with manageable muscular loads and low injury risks in different exercise modalities is
 inﬂuenced both by mechanical factors and by muscular state and coordination, which interrelate in optimizing power production
 while reducing friction and/or drag. Consequently, the choice of exercise modality in endurance training inﬂuences effort beyond
 commonly used external and internal load measurements and should be considered alongside duration, frequency, and intensity
 when managing training load. By comparing effort-matched low- to moderate-intensity sessions performed by top-level athletes
 in endurance sports, this study exempliﬁes how endurance exercise with varying modalities leads to different tolerable volumes.
 For example, the weight-bearing exercise and high-impact forces in long-distance running put high loads on muscles and
 tendons, leading to relatively low training volume tolerance. In speed skating, the ﬂexed knee and hip position required for
 effective speed skating leads to occlusion of thighs and low volume tolerance. In contrast, the non-weight-bearing, low-
 contraction exercises in cycling or swimming allow for large volumes in the speciﬁc exercise modalities. Overall, these
 differences have major implications on training load management in sports.

{
 "id":"Q96",
 "sourceFile":"The Influence of Post-Exercise        Cold-Water Immersion on Adaptive Responses to Exercise- A Review of   the      Literature.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title 'The Influence of Post-Exercise Cold-Water Immersion on Adaptive Responses to Exercise: A Review of the Literature' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain":"Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains":["Recovery & Readiness","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Athletic Training","Sports Medicine","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Narrative review of post-exercise cold-water immersion (CWI) and adaptation to training, based on a keyword search of Scopus (1963 to December 2017) plus reference lists. Single-session studies show short-term rises in PGC-1a mRNA after CWI but little or no change in the proteins it regulates. Regular CWI during endurance training showed little or no effect on mitochondrial markers and mixed effects on performance, and regular CWI during resistance training attenuated strength or muscle mass gains in some studies but not others.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Narrative review rather than a systematic review: one database, keyword search, no protocol and no formal quality appraisal of included studies. Much of the mechanistic evidence comes from small human samples (mostly 8 to 21 men) and rodent work, and many protocols used single-limb immersion or training frequencies below those of athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Reading the short-term rise in PGC-1a mRNA after cold immersion as proof that CWI improves training adaptation, or treating the review's proposed molecular mechanisms as established.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2018,
   "citation":"Broatch JR, Petersen A, Bishop DJ. The Influence of Post-Exercise Cold-Water Immersion on Adaptive Responses to Exercise: A Review of the Literature. Sports Med. 2018.",
   "doi":"10.1007/s40279-018-0910-8",
   "abstract":"Post-exercise cold-water immersion (CWI) is widely used to reduce fatigue and speed recovery between sessions, but reports suggest it may attenuate long-term adaptations. This review examines the molecular mechanisms by which CWI may alter signalling and adaptation in human skeletal muscle, focusing on mitochondrial biogenesis and muscle protein turnover. Single sessions of CWI may increase markers of mitochondrial biogenesis in the short term, but regular CWI has little to no effect on endurance adaptations, and evidence for resistance training suggests either no effect or a negative effect on strength and muscle mass.",
   "tldr":"Cold-water immersion after exercise can raise short-term markers of mitochondrial biogenesis, but regular use has little effect on endurance adaptations and may blunt strength and muscle gains after resistance training. Avoid routine use where long-term adaptation is the goal; consider it when faster recovery between sessions is the real need.",
   "methods":"Narrative review. A Scopus search using the keywords cold, skeletal muscle and exercise covered abstracts from 1963 to December 2017, and reference lists of included articles were searched. Articles were included if they addressed molecular mechanisms by which cold given during or after exercise alters skeletal muscle responses, including intracellular signalling, gene transcription and protein translation related to mitochondrial biogenesis and protein turnover.",
   "findings":"After a single endurance session, CWI increased PGC-1a mRNA in the cooled limb (up to about 9-fold in some studies), but other mitochondrial mRNA and protein markers showed no change within about 3 hours. Regular CWI during endurance training (3 to 6 weeks) had negligible or slightly beneficial effects on cycling performance in several studies, while one study using colder immersion (5 degrees C) found attenuated endurance and maximal oxygen uptake. Regular CWI during resistance training attenuated strength and muscle mass gains in some studies (including Roberts et al., 21 men, 12 weeks), but had no detrimental effect in others.",
   "limitations":"Many included studies immersed only one limb, used a single exercise or lower-body training only, and trained at 2 to 3 sessions per week, below the load of many athletes. Results differ between studies with similar protocols, and the authors note that some proposed mechanisms are speculative and unverified. Some cited molecular work is limited to small human samples and animal models, and the review was not systematic.",
   "practicalImplications":"Where the goal is endurance mitochondrial adaptation, the review gives no reason to add CWI to training. Where the goal is strength or muscle mass after resistance training, it gives no reason to add CWI and some reason for caution. CWI may still be worth considering when recovery between closely spaced sessions is the limiting factor, but the review did not test this and the authors describe it as untested.",
   "athleteDev":"Use cold immersion for short-term between-session recovery when that is the actual constraint, rather than as a routine after every strength or endurance session. The review found no study showing that regular CWI improves strength, muscle mass or mitochondrial adaptation, and some showing it may blunt strength or muscle gains.",
   "rtp":"It does not address return to sport or rehabilitation. The studies concern healthy exercisers' training adaptations; the review's background statement that CWI may reduce soft-tissue injury effects is not tested by the included evidence, so it cannot guide rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions."
 }
}

import json, os, sys

ROOT = "/Users/kristinarash/Library/Caches/sportsci-batch-98"
inputs = {x["id"]: x for x in json.load(open(os.path.join(ROOT, "inputs.json")))}


def load(i):
    return json.load(open(os.path.join(ROOT, "drafts", f"{i}.json")))


def save(i, rec, status, changes, concerns, prio):
    assert rec["sourceFile"] == inputs[i]["sourceFile"], i
    rec["verification"] = {
        "status": status,
        "changes": changes,
        "residualConcerns": concerns,
        "spotCheckPriority": prio,
    }
    s = json.dumps(rec, ensure_ascii=False, indent=1)
    assert "—" not in s, f"em dash in {i}"
    with open(os.path.join(ROOT, "verified", f"{i}.json"), "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(s + "\n")


# Q89
r = load("Q89")
save("Q89", r, "VERIFIED", [], "", "normal")

# Q92
r = load("Q92")
save("Q92", r, "VERIFIED", [],
     "", "high")

# Q95
r = load("Q95")
save("Q95", r, "VERIFIED", [], "", "normal")

# Q90
r = load("Q90")
r["paper"]["citation"] = ("Anthis M, Gourd S, Kim B, Ruddy JD, Whiteley R, Timmins R, et al. "
                          "The Fragility Index of Risk Factors for Hamstring Injuries. "
                          "J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2024;54(10):672-678.")
save("Q90", r, "CORRECTED",
     ["paper.citation: listed 3 authors before et al. -> first 6 of the 9 printed authors before et al., per house rule (byline 'MATTHEW ANTHIS ... ROD WHITELEY ... RYAN TIMMINS ... DAVID A. OPAR')"],
     "", "normal")

# Q91
r = load("Q91")
r["sports"] = ["Combat Sports", "American Football", "Mixed / General Sport"]
save("Q91", r, "CORRECTED",
     ["sports: omitted American Football -> added, since one of the three appraised studies tested professional football players ('Kiesel et al3 used a cohort design where participants were stratified into 2 groups (football lineman, football non-lineman)')"],
     "Table 2 (characteristics of the three included studies) is unreadable OCR in the extracted text, so study-level details (samples, programme lengths, populations) beyond what the narrative states could not be checked; the MMA population for Bodden et al rests on the reference title. Healthy Athletes tag is kept because inclusion required no current injury, but the Frost et al population is not stated in readable text.",
     "high")

# Q93
r = load("Q93")
p = r["paper"]
p["findings"] = ("No study has examined daylight exposure directly on the prevalence or rehabilitation of sports injuries. "
                 "Related findings include: in high-performance athletes, 10 days of winter sunlight nearly matched a 6-week regimen of 6000 IU/day vitamin D for raising serum 25(OH)D and testosterone (Michalczyk et al. 2020); "
                 "in two groups of ten male athletes, light exposure timed to the circadian rhythm had large effects on sleep duration after long-haul travel compared with no intervention, with small to moderate effects on jump and sprint measures (Fowler et al. 2021); "
                 "and in non-athletes, sunlight and supplementation both raised 25(OH)D without a change in athletic performance (Carswell et al. 2018).")
p["limitations"] = ("Not a systematic search, and no quality appraisal of included studies. "
                    "Most evidence comes from non-athletes, animal models or very small samples (the cited studies of daylight and sleep in clinical populations had one to 20 participants). "
                    "The authors note that most vitamin D and testosterone work has been done in males, so no conclusions can be drawn for females. "
                    "The Table 1 effects come from studies that were not of injured athletes in rehabilitation, and the proposed protocol has not been evaluated.")
p["athleteDev"] = ("Light timing is worth a small pilot rather than adoption as a performance tool. "
                   "Evidence for better sleep and jump or sprint measures after circadian-timed light comes from one small study of male athletes, and vitamin D findings differed between athletes and non-athletes, so keep it alongside routine sleep and nutrition care and record sleep and performance if it is trialled.")
save("Q93", r, "CORRECTED",
     ["paper.findings: Fowler et al sample given as 'ten male athletes' -> two groups of ten male athletes, circadian-timed light vs no intervention ('two groups of ten male athletes, one group receiving light exposure adapted to the individual circadian rhythm, and the other with no intervention')",
      "paper.limitations: 'the sleep studies cited range from one to 20 participants' -> the daylight and sleep studies in clinical populations (Parkinson's, glaucoma, Alzheimer's, musculoskeletal disease) had one to 20 participants ('small participant numbers ranging from one to 20')",
      "paper.limitations: 'Table 1 effects come from healthy or non-injured samples' (sample health not stated) -> from studies that were not of injured athletes in rehabilitation ('there are no existing studies on the impact of daylight on the psychological and sleep parameters of athletes in rehabilitation')",
      "paper.athleteDev: 'vitamin D findings in athletes are mixed' -> findings differed between athletes (Michalczyk) and non-athletes (Carswell); 'small studies' -> one small study (Fowler et al.)"],
     "", "high")

# Q94
r = load("Q94")
r["evidenceSummary"] = ("Descriptive repeated-measures observational study of 39 male under-19 outfield soccer players from two teams, followed over two consecutive microcycles. "
                        "GNSS acceleration and deceleration counts were recorded for each session, countermovement jump (CMJ) and isometric hamstring strength were measured before and after training, and DOMS was rated each morning. "
                        "Post-training CMJ and hamstring strength were lower than pre-training on every day, with the largest drops on MD-4 and MD-5 (about 8% each), and DOMS peaked on MD-3. "
                        "No daily acceleration or deceleration count correlated significantly with the pre-post change in CMJ or hamstring strength.")
p = r["paper"]
p["limitations"] = ("Observational design with no control group, so the findings describe association only. "
                    "The sample is modest, restricted to two youth male teams, and chosen by convenience; daily values were averaged across the two weeks, only two trials per test were used, and only acceleration and deceleration counts were analysed. "
                    "The text has internal inconsistencies: it says MD-5 sessions produced relatively few accelerations and that pre-training MD-5 CMJ and HS were lower than MD-1 to MD-4, but Tables 1 and 3 show MD-5 pre-training values close to MD-1 and the second-highest acceleration counts; table values are reported here. "
                    "Planned next-day DOMS correlations are not reported, and the MD-5 correlation trends did not reach significance.")
save("Q94", r, "CORRECTED",
     ["evidenceSummary: DOMS described as measured before and after training -> rated once each morning ('Athletes completed the scale individually each morning in their rooms, prior to breakfast')",
      "paper.limitations: added the text/table conflicts (Methods: MD-5 'generating relatively few accelerations or decelerations' vs Table 3 MD-5 37.72; Results: pre-training MD-5 'significantly lower than MD-1, MD-2, MD-3, and MD-4' vs Table 1 MD-5 CMJ 34.66 cm) and the unreported next-day DOMS correlations ('correlations were also analyzed between accelerations and decelerations on a given day and DOMS scores on the following day'); condensed the remaining limits"],
     "Several internal inconsistencies in the paper (MD-5 load description, pre-training MD-5 comparisons, DOMS MD-2 mean 0.27 in text vs 0.23 in Table 2) make the day-by-day post hoc claims less reliable; the abstract also says DOMS was measured before and after training, which the Methods contradict.",
     "high")

# Q96
r = load("Q96")
r["evidenceSummary"] = ("Narrative review of post-exercise cold-water immersion (CWI) and adaptation to training, based on a keyword search of Scopus (1963 to December 2017) plus reference lists. "
                        "Single-session studies show short-term rises in PGC-1a mRNA after CWI, but two studies found no change in PGC-1a protein up to 3 hours later. "
                        "Regular CWI during endurance training showed little or no effect on mitochondrial markers and mixed effects on performance, and regular CWI during resistance training attenuated strength or muscle mass gains in some studies but not others.")
p = r["paper"]
p["tldr"] = ("Cold-water immersion after exercise can raise short-term markers of mitochondrial biogenesis, but regular use has little effect on endurance adaptations and may blunt strength and muscle gains after resistance training. "
             "There is no adaptation-based reason to add routine CWI, and some reason for caution in strength or hypertrophy blocks.")
p["findings"] = ("After a single endurance session, CWI increased PGC-1a mRNA in the cooled limb (up to about 9-fold), but two studies found no change in PGC-1a protein content up to 3 hours after exercise. "
                 "Regular CWI during endurance training (3 to 6 weeks) had negligible or slightly beneficial effects on cycling performance in several studies, while one study using colder immersion (5 degrees C) found attenuated endurance and maximal oxygen uptake. "
                 "Regular CWI during resistance training attenuated strength and muscle mass gains in some studies (including Roberts et al., 21 men, 12 weeks), but had no detrimental effect in others.")
p["practicalImplications"] = ("Where the goal is endurance mitochondrial adaptation, the review gives no reason to add CWI to training. "
                              "Where the goal is strength or muscle mass after resistance training, it gives no reason to add CWI and some reason for caution. "
                              "Whether CWI changes adaptation when recovery between closely spaced sessions is limited has not been tested, so the review cannot settle that case.")
p["athleteDev"] = ("Avoid making cold immersion a routine after every strength session, since some studies show blunted strength or muscle gains. "
                   "The review found no study showing that regular CWI improves strength or muscle mass, and no conclusive evidence that it increases mitochondrial content or function.")
save("Q96", r, "CORRECTED",
     ["evidenceSummary and paper.findings: 'little or no change in the proteins it regulates' / 'other mitochondrial mRNA and protein markers showed no change within about 3 hours' -> two studies found no change in PGC-1a protein content up to 3 h ('two studies reporting no change in content up to 3 h after exercise')",
      "paper.tldr, practicalImplications, athleteDev: advice to use CWI when between-session recovery is the constraint -> removed as unsupported; the review states this is untested ('It remains to be determined whether CWI alters training adaptations in situations where recovery between training sessions may be limited')",
      "paper.athleteDev: 'no study showing that regular CWI improves ... mitochondrial adaptation' -> no conclusive evidence for increased mitochondrial content or function ('conclusive evidence for CWI-induced increases in the content of proteins associated with mitochondrial biogenesis ... is lacking'; one study reported slightly beneficial performance effects)"],
     "", "high")

print("ok")
